entry.title: The harbour at low tide: a field trip plan

link.title: The harbour at low tide: a field trip plan

entry.content: The spring low tide uncovers most of the harbour floor. This plan covers timing, safety, groups of five and a worksheet the pupils can finish back in class.
entry.summary: A two-hour trip for thirty pupils, with a risk checklist and a worksheet.

entry.title: Lesson 1: Why the tide comes in

link.title: Lesson 1: Why the tide comes in

entry.content: Start with a question: where does the water go? Then a model with a bucket and a torch. End with each pupil drawing the Moon’s pull in their own way.
entry.summary: The Moon, the Sun and a bucket of water: the first lesson of the unit.

entry.title: Lesson 2: Reading a tide table
entry.content: Pupils pick a day, read the high and low waters, and draw the day as a wave. Then they plan a safe time to visit the beach.
entry.summary: Turning a page of numbers into a story about one day at the harbour.

entry.title: Keeping a commonplace book with your class

link.title: Keeping a commonplace book with your class

entry.content:
A commonplace book is a notebook of things worth keeping. My class keeps one together: questions, facts and drawings.1 Here is how it works.

The rules

  1. Write the date before anything else.
  2. Copy the source with every note, even a page number.
  3. Never delete an entry; cross it out instead.

Question - any pupil can add one, with their initials.

Answer - added later, by anyone who finds it.

A worked example

Question Answered by Notes
Why is the sea salty? MK, Year 6 with a diagram
Do fish sleep? the whole class still arguing
How deep is the harbour? the harbour master 6 metres

A good question is worth more than a quick answer.

When the notes moved to a computer I wrote a tiny script to rebuild the index:

Why is the sea salty?      answered  p. 4
Do fish sleep?             open      p. 9
How deep is the harbour?   answered  p. 12

  1. The first book is now in the school library. ↩
entry.summary: How my pupils keep a shared notebook of questions, and why it works.

entry.title: Lesson 3: Mapping the shore
entry.content: Two maps of the same beach, six hours apart. The difference is the lesson.
entry.summary: Pupils draw a map of the beach at low tide, then again at high tide.

entry.title: Teaching with old paintings
entry.content: I show the class a print of a giant wave and ask one question: could this happen here? Forty minutes later, we have covered wind, depth and safety.
entry.summary: A famous print of a wave starts the best science conversations I have had.

entry.title: Notes for parents’ evening
entry.content: Ask your child to explain the tide to you. If they can, they have learned it. If they cannot, the bucket experiment works in a bath.
entry.summary: What we are learning this term, and how to help at home.
